headline: Ancient Neanderthals May Have Used Tree Tar as Medicine
meta_description: Researchers recreate prehistoric birch tar and discover it inhibits dangerous wound infections, suggesting Neanderthals used it as medicine thousands of years…
summary_short: Scientists recreated ancient birch tar production and found it kills bacteria that cause wound infections—hinting Neanderthals knew its healing power.
body:
For decades, archaeologists assumed Neanderthals used birch tar only as glue to attach stone blades to wooden handles. But new research from the University of Cologne, University of Oxford, University of Liège, and Cape Breton University suggests this sticky substance made from heated birch bark served a second, far more remarkable purpose: as an ancient antibiotic. When researchers recreated prehistoric production techniques and tested the resulting tar, every sample successfully inhibited the growth of Staphylococcus aureus, a bacterium commonly responsible for dangerous wound infections. The findings, published in PLOS One, reveal that Neanderthals may have recognized and intentionally used birch tar to protect wounds from infection thousands of years before modern antibiotics existed.

The researchers experimented with two methods archaeologists believe Neanderthals employed to produce birch tar. One involved placing birch bark in a sealed underground pit and heating it with little or no oxygen—a process called dry distillation. The other, simpler technique required burning birch bark near a cool stone surface, allowing tar vapors to condense and collect. Remarkably, both methods produced tar with identical antibacterial properties, suggesting Neanderthals would have benefited from these properties regardless of their production approach.

While the experiments cannot prove Neanderthals actually applied birch tar to wounds, the discovery aligns with growing archaeological evidence that they practiced forms of medical care and used plants intentionally. Beyond illuminating prehistoric human behavior, this research points toward a hopeful direction for modern medicine. As antibiotic resistance grows into a serious global health concern, ancient materials and traditional remedies deserve scientific investigation—reminding us that solutions to contemporary problems sometimes lie in the wisdom of the distant past.
quick_facts: Birch tar inhibited growth of Staphylococcus aureus bacteria in all tested samples
Researchers from four universities collaborated on the study published in PLOS One
Two ancient production methods—sealed pit heating and surface condensation—both worked
Traces of birch tar found at numerous Neanderthal sites across Europe
Evidence suggests Neanderthals practiced medical care and used plants intentionally
